title: Phishing the THAAD contractors
review_note: Rewritten in plain language. Core facts re-checked Oct 2026 against the DOJ release, Newsweek, SecurityWeek, PBS/AP and CyberScoop. The full complaint PDF was not read directly; affidavit details come from partial OCR and press coverage of it.

scenes.label: A job offer that was a trap
scenes.narration: [dramatically] North Korean hackers sent fake job offers to the people building America's missile shield. [short pause] That's what the FBI says. [softly] It began in 2016. A worker at an American defense company got an email. It came from a recruiter at a rival firm. A great new job was waiting. [serious] But the recruiter wasn't real. The email was bait.

visuals.text: A dream job, offered by email

scenes.label: The shield that stops missiles
scenes.narration: [calmly] So what is THAAD? It's a system that shoots down enemy missiles. It hits them high in the sky, as they fall toward their target. Lockheed Martin, one of America's biggest weapons makers, leads the building of it. The plan was to set it up in South Korea. Right next door, North Korea kept testing missiles. [short pause] So the people who built it knew secrets other countries wanted.

visuals.query: THAAD interceptor launch Missile Defense Agency

scenes.label: Coders in a Chinese port city
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Across the sea, in the Chinese port city of Dalian, a company called Chosun Expo sold coding work. North Korean programmers worked there. One was Park Jin Hyok. Investigators say he worked for the company for more than ten years. On paper, it was a normal tech business. But the US government says it was a front. It was tied to Lab 110, a North Korean military spy unit.

scenes.label: The crew with a long record
scenes.narration: Security experts call this crew the Lazarus Group. By 2016, the US says, it already had a long record. In November 2014, it hacked Sony Pictures. In February 2016, it stole $81 million from Bangladesh's central bank. Now, according to prosecutors, it picked a new kind of target. Not a movie studio. Not a bank. [pause] America's defense companies.

visuals.text: A brand new kind of target

scenes.label: Bait made just for you
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Before you trick someone, you need to know them. The FBI says these hackers did their homework. Someone on a North Korean internet address visited Lockheed Martin's websites. They looked up Lockheed workers and studied people on social media. Then came the bait, called spear-phishing. A normal scam email goes to thousands of people. Spear-phishing aims at one person. The hackers made accounts in the names of recruiters. Then they wrote to workers at rival companies.

data.subject: A role made for you
data.line: Take a look at the file

scenes.label: THAAD named in the bait
scenes.narration: Some of these emails, the Justice Department says, mentioned THAAD by name. [serious] In May 2017, the shield was set up in South Korea. That summer, North Korea launched missiles on July 4 and July 28. Newsweek reported they might reach the western United States. Right then, Palo Alto Networks, a security company, found fake job ads that hid malware. That means harmful software. One ad was for a manager on the THAAD program.

visuals.text: Palo Alto finds fake job ads

scenes.label: The door that held
scenes.narration: [surprised] At Lockheed Martin, the answer was no. The Justice Department says the attempts to break into Lockheed's computers did not succeed. [exhales] In hacking stories, that's a rare happy ending. But there's a lot we still don't know. The government hasn't said what stopped them. It hasn't said how many emails went out. [serious] The hackers had failed here. But they had left clues behind.

scenes.label: One hundred search warrants
scenes.narration: FBI agents in Los Angeles had been chasing this crew since the Sony hack. The case grew and grew. In the end, agents used about 100 search warrants. Those let them look inside roughly 1,000 email and social media accounts. [cautiously] And they found clues tying the job emails to Sony. Some used the same fake names and accounts. Some were opened from North Korean internet addresses. Different target. Same crew.

scenes.label: The fake name that slipped
scenes.narration: Then the hackers' cover started to slip. They used a fake name online: Kim Hyon Woo. Park also had his own real accounts for his normal job. Investigators say the two worlds touched. Both email names started with the same three letters, tty. Each account was saved in the other's address book. And both were reached from some of the same internet addresses. [short pause] Two strangers kept using the same front door.

scenes.label: A résumé and a big mistake
scenes.narration: Then agents found Park's résumé. It said he worked as a developer. One skill was a coding language called Visual C++. Agents say that's the language used to build many Lazarus tools. [sarcastic] For a man accused of hiding behind fake names, he left a very real paper trail. Eric Chien of the security company Symantec called it "a lack of opsec." Opsec means keeping secret work apart from real life. [short pause] Park, the FBI says, didn't.

visuals.text: a lack of opsec - Eric Chien

scenes.label: Charged, but out of reach
scenes.narration: On June 8, 2018, prosecutors in Los Angeles filed charges in secret. On September 6, they made them public. Park Jin Hyok was charged with two crimes: computer fraud and wire fraud. The worst carries up to 20 years in prison. Prosecutors also tied the crew to WannaCry, a 2017 attack that locked up computers worldwide. The Treasury put sanctions on Park. [serious] FBI Director Christopher Wray named the North Korean government as the force behind it.

visuals.text: destructive global cyber campaign - Christopher Wray

scenes.label: The job offer that never stopped
scenes.narration: Park has never been arrested. The two countries have no deal to hand over suspects. So he's on the FBI's Most Wanted list, far out of reach. North Korea denies any role. [reflective] The trick never really went away. In 2020, McAfee reported more fake job offers aimed at defense and aerospace workers. [softly] So if a stranger offers you a dream job… read it twice. If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

facts.claim: In 2016-2017 the conspiracy sent spear-phishing emails to US defense contractors including Lockheed Martin, prime contractor for THAAD; some emails purported to be from recruiters at competing contractors and some referenced THAAD, deployed in South Korea
Attempts to breach Lockheed Martin were unsuccessful
Park Jin Hyok worked for over a decade for Chosun Expo Joint Venture, affiliated with Lab 110, a component of North Korean military intelligence; researchers call the team Lazarus Group
Park worked among a team of North Korean programmers employed by Chosun Expo in Dalian, China, on paid programming/IT projects
Subjects using North Korean IP Address #6 visited websites of intended victims such as Lockheed Martin while researching Lockheed personnel and messaging employees
Subjects created accounts in names of recruiters or high-profile personnel at one company to send recruitment messages to employees of competitors such as other defense contractors
Defense-contractor emails used aliases/accounts seen in the Sony attack, sometimes accessed from North Korean IPs, and malware with the same distinct data table as Sony and bank malware
Successful attacks were preceded by reconnaissance of targets online and in social media, including Lockheed Martin employees

In July 2017 Palo Alto Networks reported Lazarus-linked malicious job-ad lures targeting US military contractor employees; one fake ad was for a management position involving THAAD; North Korean missile tests on July 4 and July 28; Hwasong-14 ICBM; THAAD deployed in South Korea May 2017
Investigators filed 100 search warrants covering about 1,000 email and social media accounts; affidavit 179 pages by FBI Special Agent Nathan P. Shields, Los Angeles
Kim Hyon Woo persona linked to Park via shared 'tty' account names, address-book entry, archive access, and common IP addresses; resume listed developer work and Visual C++
Eric Chien of Symantec described Park's account reuse as 'a lack of opsec'; complaint filed June 8, 2018

Charges unsealed September 6, 2018: conspiracy to commit computer fraud and abuse (max 5 years) and conspiracy to commit wire fraud (max 20 years); OFAC sanctioned Park and KEJV; Wray quote; WannaCry hit hundreds of thousands of computers and the UK NHS
US and North Korea have no extradition agreement
Park is on the FBI Most Wanted list
North Korea denied involvement; incident categorized as espionage against Lockheed Martin
North Korean hackers continued using fake job-recruitment emails against aerospace and defense workers (2020)

Park worked at KEJV's offices in Dalian, Liaoning, China; shared 'tty' account names, address-book entries, archive access and common IP addresses linked the Kim Hyon Woo persona to Park; resume listed Visual C++, the language used to create many Lazarus tools
Complaint filed under seal June 8, 2018 in Los Angeles and unsealed September 6, 2018
Defense-contractor spear-phishing used the same aliases and accounts as the Sony attack; John Demers called it one of the most complex and longest cyber investigations the department has taken
In July 2020 McAfee reported suspected North Korean hackers posing as job recruiters to target aerospace and defense workers
The Lazarus-linked conspiracy hacked Sony Pictures in November 2014 and stole $81 million from Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, according to the Justice Department complaint

seo.youtube_title: How North Korea Tried to Hack America's Missile Shield (THAAD)
seo.youtube_description:
How North Korea tried to hack the company behind THAAD, America's missile shield, using fake job offers from recruiters who didn't exist. The true story of the Lazarus Group, Lockheed Martin and one man the FBI says left a very real paper trail.

In 2016 and 2017, the US Justice Department says, North Korean hackers sent fake recruiting emails to workers at American defense companies, including Lockheed Martin, the main builder of the THAAD missile defense system. Some of the emails even mentioned THAAD by name. The hackers studied their targets online first. But at Lockheed Martin, the break-in attempts failed.

FBI agents in Los Angeles used about 100 search warrants to dig through roughly 1,000 accounts. The clues led to Park Jin Hyok, a North Korean programmer who worked for a front company in Dalian, China. A fake name, shared accounts and a real résumé helped tie him to the same crew blamed for the Sony Pictures hack and the $81 million Bangladesh Bank heist. He was charged in September 2018. He has never been arrested.
